classes.qualifier-missing-from-name: the definition adds an identifying attribute the name lacks (normalisation, a vector or component where the name states a scalar, an ion-only population where the name states an element, a reference-relative value, an equivalent-electron count, an averaged form, extra weighting), so the name alone denotes a broader or different quantity
classes.definition-narrower-than-name: the definition restricts applicability to a subset of the objects the name covers (a coil family, an instrument, a plasma regime or surface, a layer)
classes.abstract-parent-as-quantity: the definition declares a parent, umbrella or structural quantity whose population, component, averaging or specialised forms are fixed by more specific instances
classes.unit-does-not-fit-name: the unit's physical dimension contradicts the quantity the name states
classes.agrees: the definition states the same scope the name states

items.name: toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_internal_transport_barrier
items.description:
Toroidal carbon velocity at an internal transport barrier is the signed
toroidal component of the carbon impurity-ion fluid velocity in the
right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame, evaluated on the barrier flux
surface. At species level it is the density-weighted mean over all carbon
charge states.
items.documentation:
Toroidal carbon velocity at an internal transport barrier is the signed
toroidal component of the carbon impurity-ion fluid velocity in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, evaluated on the flux surface
identified as the internal transport barrier. For the species-level carbon
quantity, it is the density-weighted mean over all carbon ion charge states
present at that surface.

The charge-state aggregation is defined by

$$
v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}} = \frac{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}\,v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}^{q+}}}{\sum_q n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}}
$$

where $q$ indexes carbon ion charge states, $n_{\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is the
local number density of carbon ions in charge state $q+$ at the
internal-transport-barrier flux surface, and $v_{\phi,\mathrm{C}^{q+}}$ is
the corresponding toroidal fluid-velocity component.

This quantity is a local value on the internal-transport-barrier flux
surface, not a flux-surface average; a flux-surface-averaged quantity must
be named explicitly. It excludes poloidal and cylindrical-radial velocity
components, total speed, and charge-state-resolved carbon velocities. The
denominator of the aggregation is the [carbon density at the internal
transport barrier](name:carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier), and
the same carbon toroidal velocity evaluated at the magnetic axis is
[toroidal carbon velocity at magnetic
axis](name:toroidal_carbon_velocity_at_magnetic_axis).

Sign convention: Positive when the carbon ion fluid velocity points in the
direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed
cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

items.name: beta
items.description:
Global beta compares volume-averaged total perpendicular plasma pressure
with combined magnetic pressure; for a common pressure, 1/beta =
1/beta_toroidal + 1/beta_poloidal because B^2 = B_toroidal^2 + B_poloidal^2.
items.documentation:
Beta-family quantities are dimensionless equilibrium measures comparing
total perpendicular plasma pressure, aggregated over the plasma volume, with
a magnetic-pressure scale. The scale may be based on the toroidal field, the
poloidal field, or their combined magnitude; a normalized toroidal form
applies an additional scaling to the toroidal beta.

For a common volume-averaged pressure and orthogonal toroidal and poloidal
magnetic-field components, the component betas satisfy

$$
\frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{1}{\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}} + \frac{1}{\beta_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

where $\beta$ is the beta based on the combined magnetic field,
$\beta_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the [toroidal beta](name:toroidal_beta), and
$\beta_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the [poloidal beta](name:poloidal_beta). The
relation follows because the toroidal and poloidal fields add in quadrature
to give the squared total field strength.

This parent covers global equilibrium measures using total perpendicular
plasma pressure aggregated over the plasma volume and all populations
included in that total. It is not a local pressure ratio, a species-specific
pressure measure, or a magnetic-pressure quantity by itself.

The toroidal and poloidal children differ by the magnetic-field reference
used in the denominator. The [normalized toroidal
beta](name:normalized_toroidal_beta) is a separately scaled toroidal-beta
variant; it is not substituted for the unnormalized toroidal beta in the
reciprocal relation.

items.name: radial_outline_of_plasma_boundary
items.description:
Major-radius coordinate of each point on the plasma-boundary contour in a
poloidal cross-section.
items.documentation:
This quantity gives the major-radius coordinate associated with each point
of the plasma-boundary outline in a poloidal cross-section. It represents
the contour point locations measured from the toroidal symmetry axis rather
than a single representative boundary radius.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the major radius of a
point is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{X^2 + Y^2}
$$

where $R$ is the major-radius coordinate, $X$ and $Y$ are horizontal
Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is
the toroidal angle, and $Z$ is the vertical height. The quantity is
evaluated pointwise along the plasma-boundary contour, with no averaging or
summation over its points.

It is distinct from a flux-label quantity such as the [normalized poloidal
flux coordinate of the plasma
boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), and
it retains the full radial variation of the contour rather than reducing it
to one size parameter. The radial extrema of the outline provide the
horizontal extent used by the [minor radius of the plasma
boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

items.name: poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field
items.description:
Complex poloidal component of the first-order magnetic-field perturbation
eigenfunction in the current-free vacuum region outside the plasma boundary,
for a single toroidal Fourier mode in linear MHD stability analysis.
items.documentation:
The poloidal component of the perturbed vacuum magnetic field is the
projection of the first-order magnetic-field eigenfunction onto the poloidal
direction in the current-free exterior region, where $\nabla \times
\delta\mathbf{B} = 0$ and $\nabla \cdot \delta\mathbf{B} = 0$. In this
vacuum region the perturbation derives from a Laplace-scalar magnetic
potential, and the poloidal projection is one of the three components
characterizing the full spatial structure of the eigenfunction. The complex
representation — its [real
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part) and
[imaginary
part](name:poloidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part) together
— encodes amplitude and phase of the mode, arising from the toroidal Fourier
expansion for a single mode number $n$.

The poloidal projection is defined as:

$$
\delta B_\theta = \delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta
$$

where $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_\theta$ is the poloidal unit vector and
$\delta\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{vac}}$ is the full complex first-order vacuum
magnetic-field perturbation described by the parent
[perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field](name:perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field).

This component enters the plasma-vacuum interface matching conditions in
linear stability analysis, coupling the vacuum eigenfunction to the
plasma-region solution to determine free-boundary MHD stability. It
complements the toroidal counterpart documented in
[toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_real_part)
and
[toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part](name:toroidal_perturbed_vacuum_magnetic_field_imaginary_part)
in characterizing the angular structure of the eigenmode outside the plasma.
The eigenfunction amplitude is normalization-dependent; only its value
relative to the plasma-region solution carries physical meaning for
stability assessments.

Sign convention: Positive when $\delta B_\theta$ points in the direction of
increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

items.name: ion_charge_state_pressure
items.description:
Pressure of ions in a specified charge state combines thermal and nonthermal
random kinetic stresses without requiring an isotropic velocity
distribution.
items.documentation:
Pressure of ions in a specified charge state is the isotropic part of their
kinetic pressure tensor, including both thermal and nonthermal populations.
It represents random kinetic stress rather than bulk-flow ram stress; for an
anisotropic population, the scalar pressure is one-third of the
pressure-tensor trace.

The total pressure of the specified ion charge state combines its thermal
and fast-ion contributions additively:

$$
p_{s,c} = p_{s,c}^{\mathrm{thermal}} + p_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}
$$

where $s$ labels the ion species, $c$ labels its ionic charge state,
$p_{s,c}$ is the combined charge-state pressure,
$p_{s,c}^{\mathrm{thermal}}$ is the [thermal ion charge-state
pressure](name:thermal_ion_charge_state_pressure), and
$p_{s,c}^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the isotropic trace contribution of the
[fast-ion charge-state pressure](name:fast_ion_charge_state_pressure).

This quantity applies to one specified species and ionic charge state.
Thermal and nonthermal pressure contributions are added directly, not
density-weighted; there is no summation over other charge states or ion
species. Electron pressure is excluded, and the quantity is not restricted
to the thermal population alone.

The thermal contribution is isotropic. For a gyrotropic fast-ion population,
the scalar fast-ion contribution is one-third of the sum of its parallel
pressure and twice its perpendicular pressure. Thus, the combined scalar
pressure does not select either magnetic-field-relative component and does
not imply that those components are equal.

items.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity
items.description:
Toroidal current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed toroidal
projection of the electric current contribution associated with
magnetic-field-aligned viscous stress.
items.documentation:
Toroidal current density due to parallel viscosity is the signed local
projection of the current contribution associated with the divergence of
parallel viscous stress onto the geometric toroidal direction. Parallel
identifies the viscous-stress mechanism, not the current projection.

The defining projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame
is:

$$
j_\phi^{(\mathrm{pv})} = \mathbf{j}^{(\mathrm{pv})}\cdot\hat{\phi}
$$

where $j_\phi^{(\mathrm{pv})}$ is the toroidal current-density contribution,
$\mathbf{j}^{(\mathrm{pv})}$ is the full [current-density vector due to
parallel viscosity](name:current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity), and
$\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.
Here $R$ is the major radius measured from the symmetry axis, $Z$ is
vertical height, and the superscript $\mathrm{pv}$ identifies the
parallel-viscosity contribution.

In the magnetized edge plasma, this is a local, mechanism-resolved
contribution to [current density](name:current_density), not the total
toroidal current density or a flux-surface average. It excludes the
perpendicular-viscosity contribution, whose toroidal projection is [toroidal
current density due to perpendicular
viscosity](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_perpendicular_viscosity).

Parallel viscosity does not require its full current-density contribution to
be field aligned. The [parallel current density due to parallel
viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_parallel_viscosity) is the
magnetic-field-aligned projection of the same parent vector and is not
generally equal to this toroidal projection.

Sign convention: Positive when the parallel-viscosity current-density
contribution points toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$,
counter-clockwise when viewed from above.

items.name: iron_density_at_limiter
items.description:
Iron ion number density in the boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a
plasma-facing limiter surface, summed over all ionization stages and
excluding neutral iron atoms.
items.documentation:
Iron density at a limiter is the local number density of iron ions in the
boundary plasma immediately adjacent to a plasma-facing limiter surface. The
evaluation point is on the plasma side of the magnetic presheath or sheath
entrance, consistent with the parent
[density_at_limiter](name:density_at_limiter). Unless a single ionization
stage is specified in context, this quantity is summed over all iron charge
states from Fe$^{1+}$ to Fe$^{26+}$, excluding neutral iron atoms.

The total iron ion number density at the limiter is defined as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{Fe}} = \sum_{z=1}^{26} n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{Fe}^{z+}}$ is the local number density of iron in charge
state $z$.

Iron enters the edge plasma primarily through physical sputtering of
metallic plasma-facing components by energetic ions and charge-exchange
neutrals impacting the limiter surface. At the limiter, where open
scrape-off-layer field lines terminate on the material boundary, sputtered
iron atoms are ionized within a thin ionization front and become subject to
parallel and cross-field impurity transport. The local iron ion density at
the limiter characterizes the impurity source strength at this plasma-wall
interface and serves as a boundary condition for edge impurity transport
modeling. It connects to
[iron_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:iron_density_at_plasma_boundary) and
[iron_density_at_divertor_target](name:iron_density_at_divertor_target),
which describe the same impurity density evaluated at different
plasma-facing surfaces.

items.name: normalized_particle_mass
items.description:
Dimensionless ratio of a species’ particle mass to a positive reference
mass, preserving relative inertial scales in normalized kinetic equations.
items.documentation:
This quantity expresses the inertial mass of one particle of a specified
species relative to a strictly positive reference mass. It is the normalized
counterpart of particle mass, rather than an independent mass or mass
density.

The normalized particle mass is defined by

$$
\bar{m}_s = \frac{m_s}{m_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $m_s$ is the particle mass of species $s$ and $m_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is
the positive reference mass used by the normalization. The result preserves
the relative inertial ordering of species while removing the mass scale from
normalized equations of motion.

The reference mass must be kept fixed when comparing normalized masses;
changing it rescales all such ratios by the same factor. This quantity
excludes mass associated with a population or volume and does not represent
a mass density.

items.name: carbon_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
items.description:
Number density of carbon ions at the radial location of the internal
transport barrier, where suppressed cross-field turbulent transport enables
steep impurity density gradients to develop.
items.documentation:
Carbon density at the internal transport barrier is the local number density
of carbon ions ($Z = 6$) evaluated at the flux surface designated as the
internal transport barrier reference location. Unless a charge state is
specified separately, this quantity is summed over all carbon ionization
states from $\mathrm{C}^{1+}$ through $\mathrm{C}^{6+}$, providing the total
elemental impurity concentration at the barrier, consistent with the parent
[density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

The total carbon number density at the ITB is defined as:

$$
n_{\mathrm{C,ITB}} = \left. \sum_{k=1}^{6} n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}} \right|_{r = r_\mathrm{ITB}}
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{C}^{k+}}$ is the number density of carbon ions in charge
state $k$ and $r_\mathrm{ITB}$ is the radial coordinate of the barrier
reference surface.

Carbon enters fusion plasmas through erosion of carbon-based plasma-facing
components such as graphite limiters and divertor tiles. At an ITB, where
cross-field turbulent transport is locally suppressed, neoclassical impurity
transport can drive steep radial carbon density gradients — local
accumulation or depletion depending on the sign of the radial electric field
and density-gradient scale lengths. This quantity is inferred from
charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy or soft X-ray continuum emission
combined with atomic-physics modeling.

Carbon density evaluated at other plasma locations includes
[carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis](name:carbon_density_at_magnetic_axis),
[carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary](name:carbon_density_at_plasma_boundary),
and
[carbon_density_at_divertor_target](name:carbon_density_at_divertor_target);
the total ion number density at the same barrier position is given by
[total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier](name:total_ion_density_at_internal_transport_barrier).

items.name: radial_particle_convection_velocity
items.description:
Signed major-radius component of the effective velocity multiplying neutral
energy density in the convective energy flux of the edge plasma.
items.documentation:
Radial neutral-energy convection velocity is the effective coefficient of
the energy-density-proportional advective flux carried by neutral particles
in edge-plasma transport. It represents directed energy transport after the
diffusive contribution has been separated.

The radial convective neutral-energy flux is defined by

$$
F_{E,n,R}^{\mathrm{conv}} = U_n v_{E,n,R}
$$

where $F_{E,n,R}^{\mathrm{conv}}$ is the radial neutral-energy flux due to
convection, $U_n$ is the energy density of the specified neutral population,
and $v_{E,n,R}$ is this radial convection velocity.

The quantity applies to the neutral-energy channel, not the total-ion-energy
channel or a sum over charged-particle energy channels. Its direction is the
major-radius direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height. This direction is not generally normal to a magnetic flux surface.

The quantity excludes diffusive energy transport and need not equal the bulk
neutral flow velocity. It is distinct from the [neutral particle convection
velocity](name:neutral_particle_convection_velocity), which multiplies
neutral number density to define a convective particle flux; the
energy-channel and particle-channel coefficients need not coincide.

Sign convention: Positive when the neutral-energy convection velocity points
toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,
\phi, Z)$ frame.

items.name: vertical_displacement_of_thomson_scattering_channel_position
items.description:
Signed vertical offset applied to a Thomson-scattering channel position
relative to its static geometric location.
items.documentation:
The vertical displacement of a Thomson-scattering channel position is the
signed incremental change in that channel’s geometric location along the
vertical direction. It represents an offset from the static channel position
rather than the absolute position itself.

The displacement is defined by

$$
\Delta Z = Z_{\mathrm{actual}} - Z_{\mathrm{static}}
$$

where $\Delta Z$ is the vertical displacement, $Z_{\mathrm{actual}}$ is the
actual vertical coordinate of the channel position, and
$Z_{\mathrm{static}}$ is its static vertical coordinate.

This quantity applies to one Thomson-scattering channel position and
includes only its vertical component. It is not averaged over channels, does
not represent a plasma-wide vertical displacement, and is distinct from the
absolute [vertical coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position).

The actual vertical coordinate is obtained by adding this displacement to
the static vertical coordinate, $Z_{\mathrm{actual}} = Z_{\mathrm{static}} +
\Delta Z$.

Sign convention: Positive when the displacement is directed toward
increasing $Z$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

items.name: volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density
items.description:
Deuterium-tritium density is the volume-averaged ion number density of the
combined deuterium-tritium fuel pseudo-species, treating deuterium and
tritium as one effective species.
items.documentation:
Deuterium-tritium density is the volume-averaged ion number density of the
combined deuterium-tritium fuel-ion pseudo-species, treating deuterium and
tritium ions as one effective species. It is obtained from the local
[deuterium-tritium density](name:deuterium_tritium_density), which is summed
over all ion charge states.

The defining volume average is

$$
\bar n_{DT} = \frac{1}{V}\int_V n_{DT}\,dV
$$

where $\bar n_{DT}$ and $n_{DT}$ are number densities in m$^{-3}$, $V$ is
the specified averaging volume in m$^{3}$, and $dV$ is its volume element.
The local density satisfies $n_{DT}=n_D+n_T$, with $n_D$ and $n_T$ the
corresponding charge-state-summed deuterium and tritium ion densities.

The quantity includes only deuterium and tritium fuel ions represented by
the effective pseudo-species; neutral atoms and molecules, reaction
products, and impurity ions are excluded. Unlike the [line-averaged
deuterium-tritium density](name:line_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density), it
uses a volume measure rather than a line-of-sight average, and it supplies
the numerator of the [ratio of volume-averaged deuterium-tritium density to
volume-averaged electron
density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_deuterium_tritium_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density).

items.name: width_of_ferritic_element
items.description:
Full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s rectangular
cross-section, measured along major radius in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
items.documentation:
The quantity is the full non-negative radial extent of a ferritic element’s
rectangular cross-section, measured along the major-radius direction in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It spans the inner and outer
radial boundaries of the cross-section.

$$
w_R = R_{\mathrm{out}} - R_{\mathrm{in}}
$$

where $w_R$ is the radial extent, and $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ and
$R_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the outer and inner major-radius coordinates,
respectively, measured in meters.

This is a geometric width, not the radial coordinate of the [ferritic
element centroid](name:radial_coordinate_of_ferritic_element_centroid), the
outer boundary radius of an annular representation, or the extent in the
vertical direction. It is analogous to the [width of an iron core
segment](name:width_of_iron_core_segment).

items.name: current_density_due_to_distribution_function_driven
items.description:
Net electric current-density vector obtained by summing signed charge fluxes
from all particle populations in the full kinetic distribution, including
fast-particle and thermal back-current contributions.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the net electric current-density vector generated by the
charge-weighted particle motion represented in a full kinetic distribution.
It includes the fast-particle contribution together with the electron and
thermal-ion back-current contributions.

The current-density vector is defined by

$$
\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_s q_s \int \mathbf{v}\, f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{x})$ is the current-density vector at position
$\mathbf{x}$, $s$ indexes every included particle species or population,
$q_s$ is the signed electric charge per particle of species or population
$s$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, $f_s(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$ is its
phase-space distribution function, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume
element.

The quantity is local in space and aggregated over all represented particle
species and kinetic populations. It is not restricted to fast particles and
is not restricted to any single coordinate projection; the electron and
thermal-ion back-current contributions remain part of the total.

The toroidal component is the more specific [toroidal current density due to
distribution-function-driven
processes](name:toroidal_current_density_due_to_distribution_function_driven).
In contrast, [fast current density](name:fast_current_density) contains only
the selected fast-particle contribution and therefore does not represent
this full-distribution total.

Sign convention: Positive when the relevant component of $\mathbf{J}$ points
along the corresponding positive basis direction $\hat{R}$, $\hat{\phi}$, or
$\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

items.name: incident_neutral_internal_state_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination
items.description:
Number flux density of neutral recombination products in a specified
internal quantum state arriving at a plasma-facing wall surface.
items.documentation:
Incident internal-state neutral particle flux due to recombination is the
density of neutral atoms or molecules in a specified internal quantum state
that arrive at a plasma-facing wall surface from the plasma-facing side. It
is a particle-count flux, not an energy flux.

The incident flux density is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{inc}}^{(s)} = \frac{\mathrm{d}N_{\mathrm{inc}}^{(s)}}{\mathrm{d}A\,\mathrm{d}t}
$$

where $N_{\mathrm{inc}}^{(s)}$ is the number of incident neutral
recombination products in internal state $s$, $A$ is wall surface area, and
$t$ is time.

This quantity selects the incident direction and the specified internal
state from the state-resolved wall particle flux represented by [neutral
internal-state particle flux at wall due to
recombination](name:neutral_internal_state_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).
It excludes particles in other internal states and differs from the
state-summed [incident neutral particle flux at wall due to
recombination](name:incident_neutral_particle_flux_at_wall_due_to_recombination).

items.name: toroidal_neutral_torque_density
items.description:
Toroidal component of the plasma angular-momentum source density produced by
neutral–plasma momentum exchange, summed over all neutral internal states.
items.documentation:
Toroidal neutral torque density is the local source of plasma angular
momentum about the machine symmetry axis produced by momentum exchange with
neutral particles. It is aggregated over all neutral internal states and is
distinct from the state-resolved quantity [toroidal neutral internal-state
torque density](name:toroidal_neutral_internal_state_torque_density).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it is defined by

$$
\tau_{\phi,n}(R,\phi,Z) = R\sum_s \mathcal{R}_{\phi,n,s}(R,\phi,Z)
$$

where $R$ is major radius in m, $s$ indexes neutral internal states, and
$\mathcal{R}_{\phi,n,s}$ is the toroidal component of the momentum-exchange
force density from state $s$. The sum gives the neutral contribution to the
parent [neutral torque density](name:neutral_torque_density).

Sign convention: Positive when neutral momentum exchange increases plasma
angular momentum in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: radial_outline_of_divertor_tile
items.description:
Major-radius coordinates of points forming an individual divertor tile's
plasma-facing surface outline, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical (R,
φ, Z) frame. Each value is the non-negative perpendicular distance from the
toroidal symmetry axis, not a signed radial displacement.
items.documentation:
Major-radius coordinates of points forming an individual divertor tile's
plasma-facing surface outline are the cylindrical $R$ coordinates of the
boundary points in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where
$R$ is the perpendicular distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is
vertical height. They specify only the radial placement of the outline
points.

The major-radius coordinate of each outline point is the cylindrical radius
associated with the right-handed Cartesian $(x,y,z)$ frame whose $\hat{z}$
direction is vertical and whose toroidal symmetry axis is $x=y=0$:

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the same outline point in
the plane perpendicular to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This quantity excludes the [vertical outline of the divertor
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile) and any toroidal angular
coordinate of the same surface outline. It is not a signed displacement
along $\hat{R}$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, a
surface arclength, or a normal distance from the tile surface; as a
cylindrical radius, $R$ is non-negative.

items.name: ion_kinetic_energy_flux_at_wall
items.description:
Incident kinetic-energy power flux delivered by all plasma ions striking a
plasma-facing wall, summed over ion species and charge states and excluding
electrons and neutrals.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the ion-resolved component of the incident kinetic-energy
flux at a plasma-facing wall. It contributes to the parent kinetic energy
flux at wall and includes all incident ion species and charge states, but
excludes electron, neutral-particle, radiative, and electromagnetic
contributions.

For an outward wall normal $\hat{n}$ directed from the material into the
plasma, the flux is defined by

$$
q_{i}^{\mathrm{kin}} = \sum_s \int_{\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}<0} \frac{1}{2}m_s |\mathbf{v}|^2 (-\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{n}) f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3\mathbf{v}
$$

where $s$ indexes ion species and charge states, $m_s$ is the ion mass,
$\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_s$ is the incident velocity
distribution. The minus sign converts the inward particle velocity into a
positive arrival flux; the resulting quantity is non-negative.

items.name: poloidal_neutral_internal_state_convection_velocity
items.description:
Effective poloidal advection velocity for particle transport of a specified
neutral internal state, defined by the coefficient multiplying its number
density in the poloidal particle flux.
items.documentation:
The effective poloidal convection velocity is the coefficient describing
non-diffusive advection of particles in a specified neutral internal state.
It is the poloidal component of the [neutral internal-state convection
velocity](name:neutral_internal_state_convection_velocity), rather than a
scalar speed.

For the corresponding particle flux, the defining relation is

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol}} = n_{\mathrm{n,s}} v_{\mathrm{pol}}
$$

where $\Gamma_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the poloidal particle-flux component,
$n_{\mathrm{n,s}}$ is the number density of the specified neutral internal
state, and $v_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is this effective convection velocity.

This quantity applies to particle-density transport and excludes
coefficients for energy or momentum transport, such as the [poloidal
neutral-state energy convection
velocity](name:poloidal_neutral_state_energy_convection_velocity). The
poloidal direction is defined by increasing $\theta$ in the flux coordinates
$(\rho,\theta,\phi)$.

Sign convention: Positive when the effective particle convection is directed
toward increasing poloidal angle $\theta$.

items.name: outer_radius_of_passive_loop
items.description:
Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance from the cross-section center to its outer
conducting boundary.
items.documentation:
Outer radius of the annular cross-section of a passive conducting loop
element is the Euclidean distance, in the $(R,Z)$ plane at fixed toroidal
angle $phi$ of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, phi, Z)$ frame, from the
center of the annular conductor cross-section to its outer conducting
boundary. Here $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

The outer boundary radius is defined by the poloidal-plane distance from the
cross-section center to the selected outer-boundary point:

$$
r_\mathrm{outer} = \sqrt{(R_\mathrm{outer} - R_c)^2 + (Z_\mathrm{outer} - Z_c)^2}
$$

where $(R_c,Z_c)$ is the annulus-center position and
$(R_\mathrm{outer},Z_\mathrm{outer})$ is the outer-boundary position in the
same fixed-$\phi$ plane; all coordinate components in the equation are
measured in meters.

This quantity is the outer member of the [radius of a passive
loop](name:radius_of_passive_loop) family. Together with the [inner radius
of a passive loop](name:inner_radius_of_passive_loop), it defines the
conducting annulus; for a circular annulus, the cross-sectional area is
$A=\pi(r_\mathrm{outer}^2-r_\mathrm{inner}^2)$ and the radial thickness is
$r_\mathrm{outer}-r_\mathrm{inner}$. It is nonnegative and is not the loop
center's major-radius coordinate or a signed cylindrical component.

items.name: toroidal_current_density_due_to_fast_ion
items.description:
Toroidal current density carried by nonthermal ions is their
flux-surface-averaged toroidal charge flux, excluding electron and
thermal-ion back-currents.
items.documentation:
Toroidal current density due to fast ions is the signed electric-current
contribution carried by nonthermal ions in the toroidal direction, averaged
over a magnetic flux surface. The projection uses the right-handed
cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the symmetry
axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The defining charge-weighted velocity moment is:

$$
j_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}} = \left\langle \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{fast}}\cdot\hat{\phi}\right\rangle = \left\langle \sum_a q_a \int (\mathbf{v}\cdot\hat{\phi})f_a\,d^3v\right\rangle
$$

Here $j_{\phi,\mathrm{fast}}$ is this averaged toroidal component,
$\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the [fast-ion current-density
vector](name:current_density_due_to_fast_ion), and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit
vector toward increasing toroidal angle. The index $a$ labels included
fast-ion populations, $q_a$ is their ionic charge, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle
velocity, $f_a$ is their phase-space number-density distribution, and $d^3v$
is the velocity-space volume element. Angle brackets denote a
magnetic-flux-surface average.

All represented fast-ion populations are included, with multiple
distributions for the same species superposed. The aggregate is not
restricted to one orbit class; [toroidal trapped fast current
density](name:toroidal_trapped_fast_current_density) is its trapped-orbit
contribution, rather than an equivalent quantity.

Compensating electron and thermal-ion back-currents are excluded.
Consequently, this population-restricted, flux-surface-averaged projection
does not represent the full toroidal component of [current
density](name:current_density).

Sign convention: Positive when the flux-surface-averaged conventional
current carried by fast ions flows toward increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: electron_density
items.description:
Number density of electrons counts free electrons per physical volume,
excluding electrons bound in atoms, molecules, or ions.
items.documentation:
Number density of electron

The underlying local density is defined by

$$
n_e = \int f_e(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_e$ is the electron number density, $f_e$ is the electron
phase-space number distribution at the location and time considered,
$\mathbf{v}$ is electron velocity, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume
element. The integral extends over all velocities represented by the
distribution.

The unqualified quantity imposes no thermal or nonthermal population
restriction and specifies no particular plasma region. Electrons bound in
atoms, molecules, or ions are excluded. No line, surface, or volume
averaging is implicit.

[Thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast electron
density](name:fast_electron_density) restrict the electron population to
thermal and suprathermal electrons, respectively. [Total electron
density](name:total_electron_density) explicitly includes the complete
free-electron population, summing thermal and nonthermal contributions.

Spatially averaged forms retain this underlying number-density meaning:
[line-averaged electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density) is the
local density integrated along a specified plasma chord and divided by its
length, while [volume-averaged electron
density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) is the local density
integrated over the plasma volume inside the last closed flux surface and
divided by that volume.

items.name: hydrogen_density_at_internal_transport_barrier
items.description:
Particle number density of hydrogen ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier, summed over all protium ion
charge states and excluding neutral hydrogen. Hydrogen denotes protium, mass
number 1; the barrier is where locally reduced cross-field turbulent
transport can sustain steep fuel-density gradients.
items.documentation:
Particle number density of hydrogen ions evaluated on the flux surface
assigned to an internal transport barrier is the local density of the
hydrogen-ion population at that flux-surface location. Here hydrogen denotes
protium, $^1\mathrm{H}$, with mass number $A = 1$, distinct from deuterium
and tritium fuel isotopes.

The species-level hydrogen density is the charge-state sum

$$
n_\mathrm{H} = \sum_{q=1}^{Z_\mathrm{H}} n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}
$$

where $n_\mathrm{H}$ is the hydrogen-ion number density,
$n_{\mathrm{H}^{q+}}$ is the density of protium ions with charge state $q$,
and $Z_\mathrm{H}=1$ is the hydrogen atomic number. The neutral population
$q=0$ is excluded.

This quantity is the hydrogen isotope instance of [density at the internal
transport barrier](name:density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and an
ion-species contribution to ion density at the internal transport barrier,
without charge weighting. It is distinct from [deuterium density at the
internal transport
barrier](name:deuterium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) and from the
combined [deuterium-tritium density at the internal transport
barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier). The
internal transport barrier is the designated flux-surface location where
locally reduced cross-field turbulent transport permits steep fuel-density
gradients.

items.name: vertical_coordinate_of_constraint_position
items.description:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position gives its signed height
relative to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z)
frame.
items.documentation:
Vertical coordinate of the constraint position is its signed height relative
to the zero-height plane in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.
Here $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height parallel to the toroidal symmetry axis.

The coordinate is defined by

$$
Z = \mathbf{x}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is the position vector of the constraint position
measured from the coordinate origin, $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the unit vector
along the positive vertical direction, and the dot denotes the Euclidean
scalar product.

The quantity applies to an individual constraint position, not an average
over constraint positions or a vertical component of the constrained
physical quantity. It uses the same geometric projection as the [vertical
coordinate of a measurement
position](name:vertical_coordinate_of_measurement_position), with the locus
restricted to the constraint position.

Sign convention: Positive when the constraint position lies above the
zero-height plane along $+\hat{\mathbf{z}}$.

items.name: fast_electron_absorbed_wave_power_density
items.description:
Volumetric rate of coherent radio-frequency wave energy absorption by fast,
nonthermal electrons, including its flux-surface-averaged form.
items.documentation:
Fast-electron absorbed wave power density is the rate at which coherent
radio-frequency waves transfer energy directly to fast, nonthermal electrons
per unit physical volume. It describes local deposition and its average over
a magnetic flux surface.

The flux-surface-averaged form is defined by

$$
\overline{p}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}} = \left\langle p_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{fs}} = \left\langle \frac{dP_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}}}{dV} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}
$$

where $\overline{p}_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the flux-surface-averaged
absorbed wave power density, $p_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is its local
counterpart, $P_{e,f}^{\mathrm{abs}}$ is the wave power absorbed by fast
electrons, $V$ is physical volume, and $\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{fs}}$
denotes a flux-surface average. The subscripts $e$ and $f$ identify
electrons and the fast population, respectively.

The recipient population is restricted to fast electrons; thermal-electron
and ion absorption are excluded. The averaging aggregates spatial deposition
on the flux surface, not different recipient populations. The corresponding
ion-recipient quantity is [fast-ion power
density](name:fast_ion_power_density).

This quantity excludes launched wave power and subsequent [collisional
electron energy transfer](name:electron_power_density_due_to_collisions).
Its volume integral gives the fast-electron contribution to [absorbed wave
power](name:absorbed_wave_power); integrating the flux-surface-averaged form
over the corresponding enclosed-volume intervals gives the same
contribution.

items.name: toroidal_thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_thermalization
items.description:
Signed toroidal component of the local collisional angular-momentum transfer
rate per unit volume deposited in thermal ions by fast-particle
thermalization.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the toroidal component of the angular-momentum source
deposited in the thermal-ion population through Coulomb collisions with fast
particles undergoing thermalization. It represents only this collisional
exchange, rather than the total torque on the ions or the full
torque-density vector. The corresponding vector quantity is [thermal-ion
torque density due to
thermalization](name:thermal_ion_torque_density_due_to_thermalization).

The toroidal torque density is defined by

$$
\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{th}} = \left(\frac{\partial \ell_{\phi,\mathrm{th}}}{\partial t}\right)_{\mathrm{coll}}
$$

where $\tau_{\phi,\mathrm{th}}$ is the transferred toroidal torque density
and $\ell_{\phi,\mathrm{th}}$ is the toroidal angular-momentum density of
thermal ions. The collision subscript restricts the transfer to Coulomb
collisional exchange with the fast-particle distribution.

Sign convention: Positive when angular momentum is transferred to the
thermal ions in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

items.name: radial_coordinate_of_flux_surface
items.description:
Major-radius coordinate of a flux surface, defined as the midpoint between
its minimum and maximum major-radius values in the right-handed cylindrical
(R, φ, Z) frame.
items.documentation:
Major-radius coordinate of flux surface

In the right-handed cylindrical $(\hat{R},\hat{\phi},\hat{Z})$ basis, with
coordinate values $(R,\phi,Z)$, the surface coordinate is defined as the
midpoint of those extrema:

$$
R_{\mathrm{fs}} = \frac{R_{\min} + R_{\max}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{fs}}$ is the representative major-radius coordinate
assigned to the flux surface, $R_{\min}$ and $R_{\max}$ are the minimum and
maximum values, respectively, of $R$ over that complete surface, $R$ is
major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

The extrema are taken over the complete flux surface, and their midpoint is
the aggregation convention; this quantity is not an area-, volume-, or
flux-weighted average. It is a single surface-level value, not a pointwise
coordinate or the sequence of coordinates along the [radial outline of a
flux surface](name:radial_outline_of_flux_surface).

This quantity specializes the [major-radius
coordinate](name:radial_coordinate) to a flux surface by representing the
surface’s full range with one extrema midpoint. It differs from the
[normalized minor radius of a flux
surface](name:normalized_minor_radius_of_flux_surface), which expresses
radial position as a normalized quantity.

A surface formed by points sharing the same magnetic-flux label in a
nested-flux-surface configuration. Where $\psi(R, Z) = \mathrm{const}$,
$\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux.

items.name: flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude
items.description:
Flux-surface average of the squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude divided by the squared local magnetic-field magnitude, a metric
coefficient for equilibrium geometry.
items.documentation:
This coefficient describes the flux-surface-averaged geometric weighting of
a toroidal-flux radial coordinate by the inverse square of the local
magnetic-field magnitude.

The defining relation is

$$
\mathcal{G}_B = \left\langle \frac{|\nabla \rho_{\mathrm{tor}}|^2}{|\mathbf{B}|^2} \right\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}
$$

where $\mathcal{G}_B$ is the averaged metric coefficient,
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal-flux radial coordinate, $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and
$\langle\cdot\rangle_{\mathrm{FS}}$ denotes the average over a magnetic flux
surface.

The quantity applies to nested equilibrium magnetic flux surfaces and uses
the average of the pointwise ratio, not the ratio of separately averaged
numerator and denominator. It is nonnegative because both the gradient
magnitude and magnetic-field magnitude are squared.

It is the flux-surface-averaged form of the local [ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared magnetic-field
magnitude](name:ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_magnetic_field_magnitude).
It shares the gradient-squared geometric factor with the
[flux-surface-averaged squared toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient
magnitude](name:flux_surface_averaged_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude),
but additionally applies the pointwise inverse-square magnetic-field
weighting before averaging. It is distinct from the corresponding
major-radius denominator variant, [flux-surface-averaged ratio of squared
toroidal-flux-coordinate gradient magnitude to squared major
radius](name:flux_surface_averaged_ratio_of_square_of_toroidal_flux_coordinate_gradient_magnitude_to_square_of_major_radius).

items.name: electron_larmor_radius_normalized_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side
items.description:
Dimensionless ratio of the electron Larmor radius to its macroscopic
normalization length at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top, evaluated
with the local magnetic-field magnitude.
items.documentation:
The normalized electron Larmor radius is the dimensionless gyroradius of the
electron population evaluated at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top.
It characterizes electron orbit scale relative to the macroscopic length
prescribed by the normalization convention.

The defining relation is

$$
\rho_e^* = \frac{\rho_e}{L_{\mathrm{ref}}} = \frac{m_e v_{\perp,e}}{|q_e| B_{\mathrm{HFS}} L_{\mathrm{ref}}}
$$

where $\rho_e^*$ is the normalized electron Larmor radius, $\rho_e$ is the
electron Larmor radius, $L_{\mathrm{ref}}$ is the prescribed macroscopic
normalization length, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_{\perp,e}$ is the
characteristic electron speed perpendicular to the magnetic field, $q_e$ is
the electron charge, and $B_{\mathrm{HFS}}$ is the local magnetic-field
magnitude at the high-field-side pressure-pedestal top. The field magnitude
is the quantity represented by the [high-field-side pedestal-top
magnetic-field
magnitude](name:magnetic_field_magnitude_at_pedestal_top_high_field_side).

The quantity applies specifically to electrons and to the high-field-side
pressure-pedestal-top location. It is a local dimensionless scale ratio, not
an unnormalized Larmor radius, a magnetic-field component, or a quantity
aggregated over particle species. The normalization length and
characteristic-speed convention must be specified consistently; this
definition does not prescribe particular choices.

The [corresponding low-field-side
value](name:electron_larmor_radius_normalized_at_pedestal_top_low_field_side)
uses the same normalization concept with the low-field-side magnetic-field
evaluation. For equal characteristic electron speed and normalization
length, the two normalized radii vary inversely with their respective local
magnetic-field magnitudes.

items.name: volume_averaged_tungsten_density
items.description:
Volume-averaged number density of positively charged tungsten ions within
the plasma enclosed by the last closed flux surface, summed over all
ionization states.
items.documentation:
Volume-averaged tungsten-ion density is the spatial mean of the local
charge-state-summed density tungsten-ion density over the plasma volume
enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It includes all positive tungsten
ionization states and excludes neutral tungsten.

The volume average is defined by

$$
\langle n_{\mathrm{W}} \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}}\int_{V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}} n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $n_{\mathrm{W}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local tungsten-ion density,
$V_{\mathrm{LCFS}}$ is the enclosed plasma volume, $\mathbf{r}$ denotes
position, and $dV$ is the volume element. The local density is the sum of
the densities of all tungsten charge states from W$^{1+}$ through W$^{74+}$.

This quantity is distinct from the boundary flux-surface-averaged tungsten
density and from the impurity-abundance [ratio of volume-averaged tungsten
density to volume-averaged electron
density](name:ratio_of_volume_averaged_tungsten_density_to_volume_averaged_electron_density),
which is normalized to electron density.

items.name: ratio_of_line_averaged_electron_density_to_greenwald_density
items.description:
Dimensionless Greenwald fraction comparing the electron number density
averaged along a plasma chord with the empirical density limit set by plasma
current and effective minor radius.
items.documentation:
The Greenwald fraction measures the proximity of a confined plasma's
line-averaged electron density to its empirical Greenwald density limit.

It is defined by:

$$
f_G = \frac{\bar{n}_e}{n_G}
$$

where $f_G$ is the Greenwald fraction, $\bar{n}_e$ is the [line-averaged
electron density](name:line_averaged_electron_density), and $n_G$ is the
[Greenwald density](name:greenwald_density) determined from the
plasma-current magnitude and effective minor radius.

The numerator represents the electron population averaged along a plasma
chord; the denominator is the empirical density reference for the confined
plasma. This quantity is a global normalized ratio, not a local electron
density, a density limit itself, or an average over charge states or spatial
regions.

The fraction is the direct normalization of line-averaged electron density
by Greenwald density: values near unity indicate proximity to the empirical
reference limit, while values above or below unity indicate a line-averaged
density respectively above or below that reference.

items.name: first_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector
items.description:
Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis of the right-handed local basis (e1, e2, e3), paired with
the second coordinate to define the detector cross section.
items.documentation:
Signed coordinate of a neutron-detector outline vertex along the first local
tangential axis is the scalar displacement of that vertex from the detector
cross-section local origin projected onto $\hat{e}_1$. The right-handed
local detector basis $(\hat{e}_1,\hat{e}_2,\hat{e}_3)$ has $\hat{e}_3$ as
the plasma-facing normal to the detector cross section, $\hat{e}_1$ as the
tangential axis whose positive sense is toward increasing toroidal angle
$\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, and $\hat{e}_2 =
\hat{e}_3 \times \hat{e}_1$.

The coordinate is defined by the local tangent-plane projection:

$$
\ell_1 = (\mathbf{r}_v - \mathbf{r}_0) \cdot \hat{e}_1
$$

where $\ell_1$ is this first local tangential coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_v$ is
the position vector of the outline vertex, $\mathbf{r}_0$ is the position
vector of the detector cross-section local origin, and $\hat{e}_1$ is the
first local tangential unit vector.

Together with the [second local tangential coordinate of the neutron
detector](name:second_local_tangential_coordinate_of_neutron_detector), this
coordinate specifies the in-plane position of an outline vertex of the
detector cross section. It is not a cylindrical $R$, $\phi$, or $Z$ position
in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame and does not denote
displacement normal to the detector cross section.

Sign convention: Positive when the outline vertex is displaced from the
local origin in the $+\hat{e}_1$ direction.

items.name: poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_plasma_boundary
items.description:
Area enclosed by the last closed magnetic flux surface in a poloidal plane,
defining the equilibrium plasma cross-sectional size at the plasma boundary.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the geometric area enclosed by the last closed magnetic
flux surface (LCFS), which forms the plasma boundary, in a poloidal
cross-section.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, the enclosed area is
defined by

$$
A_{\rm LCFS} = \iint_{\mathcal{S}_{\rm LCFS}} dR\,dZ
$$

where $A_{\rm LCFS}$ is the LCFS cross-sectional area, $\mathcal{S}_{\rm
LCFS}$ is the region enclosed by the LCFS contour at fixed toroidal angle
$\phi$, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, $Z$ is vertical
height, and $dR\,dZ$ is the poloidal-plane area element.

This is a global equilibrium quantity for the complete plasma-boundary
contour. It is not a local surface element, a flux-surface average, or the
area of a toroidal surface formed by revolving the contour.

It is the plasma-boundary specialization of [poloidal plane cross-sectional
area of a flux
surface](name:poloidal_plane_cross_sectional_area_of_flux_surface), whose
corresponding area is defined for an arbitrary closed magnetic flux surface;
the LCFS is the outermost such surface enclosing the plasma.

items.name: thermal_particle_power_due_to_thermalization
items.description:
Volume-integrated net power transferred to the thermal particle population
as nonthermal particles lose energy and join the thermal background.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the net rate of energy transfer to the thermal particle
population from the thermalization of nonthermal particles. It represents
the global contribution of this process to the thermal-particle energy
balance, rather than a local power density or particle source rate.

The volume-integrated power is defined by

$$
P_{\rm th,therm} = \int_{\mathcal{V}} p_{\rm th,therm}(\mathbf{r})\,dV
$$

where $P_{\rm th,therm}$ is the integrated power in W, $p_{\rm
th,therm}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local thermalization power density in W
m$^{-3}$, $\mathbf{r}$ is position, and $\mathcal{V}$ is the plasma volume.

Positive values represent net energy gain by the thermal particle
population; negative values represent net transfer of energy from the
thermal population to a nonthermal population. The local counterpart is
[thermal particle power density due to
thermalization](name:thermal_particle_power_density_due_to_thermalization),
while particle-number transfer is represented separately by [total thermal
particle source rate](name:volume_integrated_particle_source_rate).

items.name: poloidal_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity
items.description:
Poloidal current density due to heat viscosity is the signed local charge
flux in the poloidal direction generated by heat-viscosity stresses in a
collisional magnetized plasma.
items.documentation:
Poloidal current density due to heat viscosity is the local poloidal
component of the electric-current contribution generated by heat-viscosity
stresses in a collisional magnetized-plasma fluid closure.

Its defining projection is

$$
j_{\mathrm{p}} = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}
$$

where $j_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the poloidal current density due to heat
viscosity, $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{hv}}$ is the [heat-viscosity current-density
vector](name:current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), and
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the unit vector along the designated
local poloidal direction. This direction lies in a plane of constant
toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$
is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Its
positive orientation must be specified by the local poloidal-component
convention; the heat-viscosity attribution alone does not determine it.

This is a local, unaveraged contribution to [electric current
density](name:current_density), not a surface-integrated current or the
total current density from all mechanisms. Only the heat-viscosity
contribution is included; the definition imposes no restriction to a
particular species or plasma region. The quantity is a signed directional
projection, not the magnitude of the current in the poloidal plane.

Unlike [parallel current density due to heat
viscosity](name:parallel_current_density_due_to_heat_viscosity), which
projects the same parent vector along the local magnetic field, this
quantity projects onto the designated local poloidal direction. Poloidal
therefore identifies the projection, not the orientation of the viscous
stress responsible for the current.

Sign convention: Positive when the heat-viscosity current has a component
along the designated positive local poloidal direction
$\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{p}}$.

items.name: poloidal_electron_energy_diffusivity
items.description:
Effective coefficient relating the poloidal diffusive flux of electron
thermal energy to the poloidal gradient of electron thermal-energy density
in the edge plasma.
items.documentation:
The poloidal electron energy diffusivity describes local, gradient-driven
smoothing of electron thermal-energy density in the edge plasma. It is the
poloidal specialization of the [electron energy
diffusivity](name:electron_energy_diffusivity).

The defining local closure is:

$$
Q_{e,W,\mathrm{p},\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{e,W,\mathrm{p}}\,\frac{\partial u_e}{\partial l_{\mathrm{p}}}
$$

where $Q_{e,W,\mathrm{p},\mathrm{diff}}$ is the poloidal component of
diffusive electron thermal-energy flux density, $D_{e,W,\mathrm{p}}$ is this
diffusivity, $u_e$ is electron thermal-energy density, and $l_{\mathrm{p}}$
is physical distance along the local poloidal transport direction. The minus
sign expresses down-gradient transport for a nonnegative diffusivity.

The poloidal direction runs around the magnetic axis within a plane of
constant toroidal angle in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame,
where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical
height. This differs from the field-aligned direction associated with
[parallel electron energy
diffusivity](name:parallel_electron_energy_diffusivity).

This coefficient applies locally to electron thermal energy, without spatial
averaging or aggregation with ion or neutral energy transport. It excludes
advective and convective contributions, including the contribution
parameterized by [electron energy convection
velocity](name:electron_energy_convection_velocity). It is an
energy-density-gradient coefficient, not directly a temperature-gradient
heat-transport coefficient; conversion requires the electron density,
heat-capacity factors, and their spatial dependence to be specified.

items.name: z_coordinate_of_divertor_target
items.description:
Vertical Cartesian coordinate of the geometric center of a divertor target
surface, identifying its location along the facility's vertical axis.
items.documentation:
The quantity is the vertical coordinate of the geometric center of a
divertor target surface. It identifies the center point rather than the
target's vertical extent or surface outline.

In the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ frame, the
coordinate is defined by

$$
z_{\mathrm{target}} = \mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{z}}
$$

where $\mathbf{r}_{\mathrm{target}}$ is the position vector of the target
surface center relative to the frame origin and $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is the
vertical unit vector. The $z$ direction corresponds to $Z$ in the
right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

Together with the [x coordinate of the divertor
target](name:x_coordinate_of_divertor_target) and [y coordinate of the
divertor target](name:y_coordinate_of_divertor_target), this quantity
locates the target surface center. It is distinct from the [vertical length
of the divertor target](name:vertical_length_of_divertor_target) and the
[vertical outline of the divertor
tile](name:vertical_outline_of_divertor_tile), which describe extent and
boundary geometry rather than the center position.

items.name: ion_energy_flux
items.description:
Ion energy flux is the net energy carried by ions across an oriented surface
per unit area and time, including conductive and convective transport.
items.documentation:
Ion energy flux is the signed rate of energy transport carried by an ion
population across an oriented surface per unit area. It is the transport
flux entering the ion energy balance, rather than a volume energy source or
a surface-integrated power.

The local surface flux is defined by:

$$
\Gamma_{W,i} = \boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{W,i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n} = \lim_{\Delta A,\Delta t\to 0}\frac{\Delta W_i}{\Delta A\,\Delta t}
$$

where $\Gamma_{W,i}$ is the signed ion energy flux through the surface,
$\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{W,i}$ is the underlying ion energy-flux vector, and
$\hat{\mathbf n}$ is the chosen surface unit normal. The subscript $i$
identifies the ion population, $\Delta W_i$ is the net ion energy crossing a
surface patch during the time interval $\Delta t$, and $\Delta A$ is the
patch's actual area, not its projected area.

The population may be one ion species or an aggregate of ion species. For
one species, the flux is summed over all its ionic charge states; the [ion
charge-state energy flux](name:ion_charge_state_energy_flux) resolves
individual charge-state contributions. The [total ion energy
flux](name:total_ion_energy_flux) sums over all ion species and charge
states. Energy carried by electrons or neutrals is excluded.

The flux includes conductive thermal-energy transport and convective
enthalpy or bulk-kinetic transport according to the ion energy balance
represented; it is not restricted to gradient-driven diffusion. The [energy
convection velocity](name:energy_convection_velocity) multiplies the
transported energy density to give the convective contribution, not the full
flux when conduction is also present.

The [radial](name:radial_ion_energy_flux),
[poloidal](name:poloidal_ion_energy_flux), and
[parallel](name:parallel_ion_energy_flux) ion energy fluxes select
directional projections of the same underlying energy-flux vector. The
general surface-flux definition does not select any one of these directions.

Sign convention: Positive when net ion energy crosses the surface in the
direction of its chosen unit normal.

items.name: resistance_of_poloidal_field_coil
items.description:
Ohmic resistance of an individual poloidal-field coil winding, relating its
resistive voltage drop to current and determining Joule dissipation.
items.documentation:
The ohmic resistance characterizes the opposition to electrical current in
an individual poloidal-field coil winding and the associated conversion of
electrical energy into heat.

For coil current $I$ and resistive voltage drop $V_R$, the resistance is
defined by

$$
V_R = R I
$$

where $R$ is the ohmic resistance, $I$ is the signed winding current in
amperes, and $V_R$ is the resistive voltage drop in volts.

This quantity excludes inductive back-EMF and other transient voltage
contributions represented by the [voltage of the poloidal field
coil](name:voltage_of_poloidal_field_coil). Its value may depend on the
conductor state, including the [temperature of the poloidal field
coil](name:temperature_of_coil_conductor), and is conceptually analogous to
the [resistance of the toroidal field
coil](name:resistance_of_toroidal_field_coil).

items.name: toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential
items.description:
Toroidal component of the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential,
retaining the signed projection along increasing toroidal angle for
linear-MHD mode representations.
items.documentation:
The toroidal component of the perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential is
the signed projection of the vector-potential perturbation onto the
geometric toroidal direction within the plasma. It represents the toroidal
member of the component family derived from the [perturbed plasma magnetic
vector potential](name:perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major
radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the component
is defined by

$$
\delta A_\phi = \delta\mathbf{A} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\delta A_\phi$ is the toroidal component, $\delta\mathbf{A}$ is the
perturbed plasma magnetic vector potential, and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit
vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. The associated
perturbed magnetic field is determined by $\delta\mathbf{B} = \nabla \times
\delta\mathbf{A}$, where $\delta\mathbf{B}$ is the perturbed magnetic field
and $\nabla$ is the spatial gradient operator.

This quantity applies to the plasma magnetic-vector-potential perturbation
itself and is a local toroidal component, not a species sum, charge-state
sum, surface average, or volume average. The vector potential depends on the
selected gage, whereas its curl gives the gage-invariant magnetic-field
perturbation. It is distinct from the [toroidal perturbed plasma magnetic
field](name:toroidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_field), which is the toroidal
component of $\delta\mathbf{B}$ rather than of $\delta\mathbf{A}$. The
corresponding component construction in another direction is represented by
the [poloidal perturbed plasma magnetic vector
potential](name:poloidal_perturbed_plasma_magnetic_vector_potential). For
complex linear-MHD eigenfunctions, an imaginary-quadrature specialization
retains only the imaginary part of this toroidal component.

Sign convention: Positive when $\delta A_\phi$ points in the direction of
increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

items.name: radial_total_current_density_at_wall
items.description:
Radial (R-direction) component of the total electric current-density vector
at a plasma-facing wall in the right-handed cylindrical (R, φ, Z) frame,
where R is major radius and Z is vertical height. It is signed positive
toward increasing R.
items.documentation:
Radial (R-direction) component of the total electric current-density vector
at a plasma-facing wall is the projection of the local total electric
current-density vector onto the $\hat{R}$ basis direction of the
right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame. Here $R$ is major radius
measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$
is vertical height.

The defining projection at a wall point $\mathbf{x}_w$ is:

$$
j_{R,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{wall}}(\mathbf{x}_w) = \mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}(\mathbf{x}_w) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{R}}(\mathbf{x}_w)
$$

where $j_{R,\mathrm{tot}}^{\mathrm{wall}}$ denotes this scalar quantity,
$\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is the total
[current_density](name:current_density), $\hat{\mathbf{R}}$ is the local
unit vector toward increasing $R$, and $\mathbf{x}_w$ lies on the
plasma-facing material wall.

Total means all current-carrying contributions included in the physical
current-density vector, such as inductive, neoclassical, wave-driven,
kinetic, conductive, charged-particle, and sheath-mediated currents. This
quantity is the wall-evaluated radial projection of the total vector, not a
process-resolved contribution such as
[radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction](name:radial_current_density_due_to_ion_neutral_friction).
A tile current such as
[current_of_divertor_tile](name:current_of_divertor_tile) is a surface
integral of the current-density component normal to that tile; it equals an
area integral of this radial component only where the tile normal is
parallel to $\hat{R}$.

Sign convention: Positive when $\mathbf{j}_{\mathrm{tot}}$ at the wall
points in the direction of increasing major radius $R$.

items.name: density_at_internal_transport_barrier
items.description:
Particle number density of a specified plasma population evaluated on the
flux surface assigned to an internal transport barrier, with charge-state
aggregation determined by the population.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the local number density of a selected plasma population at
the flux-surface location assigned to an internal transport barrier. It
applies to electrons, individual ion species, and compound fuel populations
treated as effective species.

The number density is defined by

$$
n = \lim_{\Delta V\to 0}\frac{\Delta N}{\Delta V}
$$

where $n$ is the number density in m$^{-3}$, $N$ is the number of counted
particles, and $V$ is volume in m$^{3}$. For an ion species, the count is
summed over its ionic charge states and excludes neutral atoms; electrons
are counted directly. The ion density at the internal transport barrier and
[electron density at the internal transport
barrier](name:electron_density_at_internal_transport_barrier) are specific
population instances, while the [deuterium-tritium density at the internal
transport
barrier](name:deuterium_tritium_density_at_internal_transport_barrier)
treats the fuel mixture as one effective population. The internal transport
barrier is the designated flux-surface location where reduced cross-field
turbulent transport permits steep density gradients.

items.name: electrostatic_potential
items.description:
Electrostatic interaction energy per positive test charge in a plasma or at
a material boundary, relative to a chosen electrical reference.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the electrostatic potential in a plasma or at a material
boundary, relative to a chosen electrical reference. It specifies
electrostatic interaction energy per positive test charge.

The defining energy relation is

$$
\Phi = \frac{\Delta U}{q}
$$

where $\Phi$ is the reference-relative electrostatic potential, $\Delta U$
is the change in electrostatic potential energy of a test charge moved from
the reference to the evaluation location, and $q$ is the positive test
charge.

The quantity applies across core plasma, edge plasma, the scrape-off layer,
and material boundaries. It may denote a local value or an explicitly
specified spatial average; no particular averaging operation or evaluation
locus is intrinsic to the general quantity. A flux-surface-averaged value is
the mean over a specified magnetic flux surface, not an assertion that the
local potential is constant on that surface.

For the local potential, the electrostatic electric field is
$\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{es}}=-\nabla\Phi$, where $\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{es}}$
denotes the electrostatic contribution to the electric field and $\nabla$ is
the spatial gradient. This relation excludes any inductive electric-field
contribution. Potential gradients therefore contribute to plasma rotation
through electric-field-cross-magnetic-field drift. Changing the electrical
reference adds a spatially constant offset without changing this electric
field.

The [potential at a Langmuir-probe
position](name:electrostatic_potential_at_langmuir_probe_position) is a
local plasma value, whereas the [floating electrostatic
potential](name:floating_electrostatic_potential) is the collector value
constrained by zero net current. A sheath can sustain a difference between
them. The [real part](name:electrostatic_potential_real_part) and [imaginary
part](name:electrostatic_potential_imaginary_part) are quadratures of a
complex representation; a fluctuation amplitude instead characterizes
magnitude, with any normalization specified separately.

Sign convention: Positive when a positive test charge has greater
electrostatic potential energy at the evaluation location than at the chosen
reference.

items.name: thermal_electron_energy
items.description:
Volume-integrated thermal energy content of the electron population,
excluding fast suprathermal electrons and non-electron plasma populations.
items.documentation:
Volume-integrated thermal energy content of the electron population is the
total kinetic energy carried by bulk thermal electrons throughout the
confined plasma. It is an extensive energy content, not a power or
energy-transfer rate, and excludes fast suprathermal electrons and
non-electron populations.

The defining relation is

$$
E_{e,\mathrm{th}} = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_\mathrm{plasma}} p_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{r})\,\mathrm{d}V
$$

where $E_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the integrated thermal electron energy,
$p_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{r})$ is the local thermal electron pressure,
$V_\mathrm{plasma}$ is the confined plasma volume, and $\mathbf{r}$ denotes
position. This quantity is the thermal-electron component of [electron
energy](name:electron_energy); unlike [thermal plasma
energy](name:thermal_plasma_energy), it excludes thermal-ion energy.

items.name: magnetic_shear_at_magnetic_axis
items.description:
Magnetic shear evaluated at the magnetic axis, defined as the limiting
normalized logarithmic derivative of the safety factor with respect to
normalized toroidal flux radius.
items.documentation:
Magnetic shear at the magnetic axis is the limiting value of [magnetic
shear](name:magnetic_shear_at_flux_surface) as the flux-surface label
approaches the magnetic axis.

Using the [normalized toroidal flux
coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate)
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ as the radial label, with
$\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}=0$ at the magnetic axis, the defining relation is

$$
s_{\mathrm{axis}} = \lim_{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}\to 0} \frac{\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}{q}\frac{dq}{d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}}
$$

where $q$ is the safety factor and $s_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-shear
limit. For a smooth equilibrium with finite [safety factor at the magnetic
axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis), this limit is zero. It therefore
differs from evaluations on finite-radius surfaces such as [magnetic shear
at the plasma boundary](name:magnetic_shear_at_plasma_boundary).

Sign convention: Positive when $q^{-1}dq/d\rho_{\mathrm{tor,norm}}$ is
positive as the normalized toroidal flux radius increases outward from the
magnetic axis.

items.name: average_charge_number
items.description:
Number-density-weighted mean ionic charge number over the charge-state
distribution of a specified ion population.
items.documentation:
This quantity is the mean ionic charge number of a specified ion population
distributed among multiple charge states.

$$
\overline{Z} = \frac{\sum_q q n_q}{\sum_q n_q}
$$

where $q$ is the integer charge number of charge state $q$, $n_q$ is the
number density of ions in that charge state, and the sums extend over the
included charge states.

The average applies to one specified ion population and uses number-density
weighting over its charge-state distribution. It is an average rather than a
sum, so it does not represent total charge density or the charge number of
one particular state; it is also distinct from the nuclear [atomic
number](name:atomic_number), which is independent of ionization state.

The [ion charge-state average charge
number](name:ion_charge_state_average_charge_number) is a concrete instance
of this charge-state-averaged quantity for the corresponding ion population.

items.name: perpendicular_runaway_electron_diffusivity
items.description:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar diffusion
coefficient governing runaway-electron spreading perpendicular to the
magnetic field and across magnetic flux surfaces.
items.documentation:
Perpendicular runaway-electron diffusivity is the effective scalar
coefficient for Fickian diffusion of runaway electrons perpendicular to the
magnetic field. In flux-surface transport descriptions, it represents the
cross-surface diffusive transport component along the flux-surface normal,
positive toward increasing flux label.

The diffusive contribution to the perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux is defined by

$$
\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}} = -D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}\,\frac{\partial n_{\mathrm{RE}}}{\partial \ell_\perp}
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ is the perpendicular runaway-electron
diffusivity, $\Gamma_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}^{\mathrm{diff}}$ is the diffusive
part of the [perpendicular runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux), $n_{\mathrm{RE}}$
is the [runaway-electron density](name:runaway_electron_density), and
$\ell_\perp$ is distance along the local flux-surface-normal direction
perpendicular to the magnetic field. The minus sign states that a positive
diffusivity gives diffusive flux from larger toward smaller runaway-electron
density.

This quantity applies only to the runaway-electron population and only to
its perpendicular diffusive particle transport. It is not a parallel
transport coefficient, not a convective velocity, and not the full
[runaway-electron diffusivity](name:runaway_electron_diffusivity) when that
broader quantity includes additional directional components.

The [perpendicular runaway-electron convection
velocity](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_convection_velocity) gives the
advective contribution to the same perpendicular particle balance, whereas
$D_{\mathrm{RE},\perp}$ multiplies the density gradient. The sum of
diffusive and convective contributions forms the modeled [perpendicular
runaway-electron particle
flux](name:perpendicular_runaway_electron_particle_flux).

items.name: ion_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer
items.description:
Radial e-folding decay length of the ion heat flux in the scrape-off layer,
defined by its outward logarithmic decrease.
items.documentation:
The ion heat decay length in the scrape-off layer (SOL) is the radial
distance over which the ion heat-flux profile falls to $1/e$ of its
separatrix value, characterizing the spatial scale of ion heat exhaust
across the open-field-line region.

The decay length is defined by the inverse magnitude of the outward
logarithmic radial gradient of the ion heat flux $q_i$:

$$
\lambda_{q,i} = \left| \frac{\partial \ln q_i}{\partial r} \right|^{-1}
$$

where $r$ is radial distance measured outward from the separatrix and $q_i$
is the ion contribution to the heat flux. This species-resolved quantity is
the ion-channel specialization of
[heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer);
the corresponding electron channel is
[electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer](name:electron_heat_decay_length_over_scrape_off_layer).
It excludes the electron heat contribution and any unspecified total
heat-flux combination.

items.name: parallel_wave_electric_field
items.description:
Complex phasor of the wave electric field projected along the local
equilibrium magnetic-field direction in a magnetized plasma.
items.documentation:
The parallel wave electric field is the complex phasor obtained by
projecting the electromagnetic-wave electric-field phasor onto the local
